items.stem: The chart shows U.S. military spending rising steeply in the early 1980s. Alongside this buildup, Reagan 'funded anti-communist insurgents' abroad — a policy often called the Reagan Doctrine. How did the doctrine fit the broader strategy the chart shows?

chart_spec.title: U.S. Military Spending, 1980–1990 (nominal)
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the Reagan-era military buildup described in u9.md §The story ('spending massively on the military abroad').

options: (A) The doctrine replaced the buildup, letting Reagan cut the military budget the chart shows rising.
(B) The doctrine was unrelated to the Cold War and concerned only Latin American trade policy.
(C) A cheaper complement to the military buildup: backing anti-Soviet guerrillas in Nicaragua and Afghanistan.
(D) The doctrine meant invading the Soviet Union with American ground troops.
items.explanation: The buildup the chart documents — spending nearly doubling by 1985 — was the direct, expensive pressure; the Reagan Doctrine was the indirect, cheaper one. Aiding the Contras against Nicaragua's Sandinistas and the mujahideen against the Soviet army in Afghanistan bled Soviet clients and the USSR itself at a fraction of the cost of American divisions.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The chart shows spending rising throughout the 1980s; the doctrine supplemented the buildup rather than replacing it.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The doctrine was explicitly anti-communist and global — Nicaragua, Afghanistan, Angola, Cambodia — not a trade policy.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It correctly describes the doctrine's mechanism and its relationship to the larger buildup: indirect pressure as the economical partner of direct military spending.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. No invasion of the USSR was ever planned; the doctrine's whole point was to avoid direct superpower combat.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Reagan 'funded anti-communist insurgents' while 'spending massively on the military abroad'

items.stem: In June 1987, standing before the Brandenburg Gate, Reagan declared: 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' In December 1987, he signed the INF Treaty with Gorbachev. How should a historian weigh the speech against the treaty?

stimulus.text: In June 1987, standing before the Brandenburg Gate, Reagan declared: 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' In December 1987, he signed the INF Treaty with Gorbachev eliminating intermediate-range missiles. (Historical facts summarized for this item.)

options: (A) The speech proves Reagan never negotiated with the Soviets at any point.
(B) The treaty proves the famous speech was never actually delivered.
(C) The speech and the treaty cancel each other out entirely, leaving historians with no usable evidence of Reagan's intentions.
(D) The speech was public rhetoric pressuring Gorbachev; the major arms treaty signed that same year shows Reagan negotiating seriously.
items.explanation: This is the review's central point about Reagan: the 'evil empire' rhetoric and the SDI pressure campaign coexisted with genuine diplomacy once Gorbachev offered a partner. The speech played to the cameras; the treaty eliminated real missiles. A historian who cites only one half misses how the strategy worked.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The INF Treaty, signed six months later, is direct evidence that Reagan did negotiate — seriously and successfully.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The speech is one of the most documented public addresses of the decade; the treaty does not erase it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The two are complementary instruments rather than contradictory evidence; historians routinely find leaders combining pressure with negotiation.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It distinguishes the speech's audience and purpose from the treaty's substance, capturing the rhetoric-versus-diplomacy duality the review describes.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Reagan 'called the Soviet Union an "evil empire"... then, when Mikhail Gorbachev came to power seeking reform, negotiated seriously, signing the INF Treaty in 1987'

items.stem: The chart shows U.S. military spending climbing from $134 billion in 1980 to $253 billion in 1985. How did Reagan's approach to the Soviet Union differ from Nixon's détente of the early 1970s?

chart_spec.title: U.S. Military Spending, 1980–1990 (nominal)
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the Reagan-era military buildup described in u9.md §The story ('spending massively on the military abroad').

options: (A) Nixon pursued coexistence through negotiated limits; Reagan paired military buildup with confrontation, then negotiated.
(B) Nixon built up the military while Reagan disarmed and cut spending.
(C) Both presidents pursued identical policies with no meaningful differences.
(D) Nixon ignored the Soviet Union entirely while Reagan sought peaceful coexistence from the very start of his presidency in 1981.
items.explanation: Détente accepted the USSR as a permanent rival to be managed through arms-control treaties and trade. Reagan rejected that premise: the chart's near-doubling of military spending by 1985 was pressure designed to change Soviet behavior, paired with 'evil empire' moralism — and only after the pressure came the serious negotiation that produced the INF Treaty.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It states the real contrast: management of the rivalry (Nixon) versus pressure-then-negotiation (Reagan), with the chart documenting the pressure phase.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the two: Nixon pursued détente-era restraint while Reagan launched the buildup the chart shows.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The chart itself evidences the difference: Reagan's spending surge broke sharply with the détente era's military restraint.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Nixon engaged the Soviets intensively (SALT, summits); Reagan began with confrontation, not coexistence.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Reagan 'called the Soviet Union an "evil empire"... then, when Mikhail Gorbachev came to power seeking reform, negotiated seriously'

items.stem: The Iran-Contra affair, exposed in 1986, involved the secret, illegal sale of arms to Iran to fund Contra rebels in Nicaragua. What did the affair most clearly reveal about the Reagan administration?
options: (A) That the administration had no interest in Central America or its conflicts.
(B) That officials pursued anti-communist goals outside the law, deceiving Congress and the public.
(C) That Congress had authorized every part of the operation in advance.
(D) That the affair actually strengthened the administration's reputation for strict and careful legal compliance.
items.explanation: Congress had cut off aid to the Contras; administration officials evaded that restriction by secretly selling arms to Iran — itself under an arms embargo — and diverting the profits. The scandal showed the tension between the administration's anti-communist zeal and constitutional limits, damaging Reagan's standing even though he survived it politically.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The affair proves the opposite: the administration cared enough about Nicaragua to break the law over it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It names what the investigations established: an off-the-books foreign policy run around Congress's explicit restrictions.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Evading Congress was the scandal's core; the operation was concealed precisely because Congress had forbidden Contra aid.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The affair produced criminal convictions of administration officials and a lasting stain on the administration's legal reputation.

items.fact_source: u9.md §Key terms — Iran-Contra affair: 'the secret, illegal sale of arms to Iran to fund Contra rebels in Nicaragua, exposed in 1986'

items.stem: The chart shows crude oil prices collapsing from about $35.50 per barrel in 1980 to the mid-$20s by the late 1980s. Why did this price collapse hurt the Soviet Union especially badly?

chart_spec.title: Crude Oil Prices, 1973–1990 (nominal dollars per barrel)
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the 1980s oil-price collapse that squeezed Soviet export revenues, an internal pressure on the USSR alongside the factors in u9.md §What the exam tests here ('internal Soviet decay').

options: (A) The Soviet Union imported all of its oil and had to pay more for it.
(B) The price collapse had no effect on the Soviet economy whatsoever, which was completely insulated from world markets.
(C) The USSR lived on oil-export earnings; the 1980s price crash cut state revenue just as the arms race demanded more spending.
(D) The Soviet Union had already stopped producing oil entirely by 1980.
items.explanation: The Soviet command economy could not produce competitive manufactured exports, so it paid for imported grain and technology with oil and gas earnings. When prices fell by roughly a third in the mid-1980s, that revenue stream shrank exactly when matching Reagan's buildup required more military spending — an internal economic squeeze that deepened the system's crisis.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The USSR was a major oil exporter, not an importer; the problem was falling export earnings, not rising import costs.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The revenue loss was severe and well documented; it compounded the stagnation Gorbachev was trying to fix.
option_explanations.C: Correct. It connects the chart's price collapse to the Soviet fiscal bind: shrinking hard-currency income meeting rising military demands.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Soviet oil production remained enormous through the 1980s; the issue was the price, not the volume.

items.fact_source: u9.md §What the exam tests here — 'internal Soviet decay' as a required cause of the Cold War's end

items.stem: In 1989, communist governments fell across Eastern Europe in rapid succession. What Soviet decision made those revolutions possible?
options: (A) The Soviet Union sent tanks into every Eastern European capital to defend the regimes, but the tanks broke down en route.
(B) Gorbachev ordered the construction of a new Berlin Wall to contain the unrest.
(C) The Soviet Union had already dissolved before 1989, so no decision was needed.
(D) Gorbachev refused to use Soviet force against the uprisings, abandoning the Brezhnev Doctrine of past invasions.
items.explanation: Eastern European regimes had survived for decades because Moscow would intervene — as in Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968). When Gorbachev made clear in 1989 that Soviet tanks would not come, the regimes' enforcers lost their nerve and crowds filled the streets. The empire's outer ring fell because its center chose not to defend it.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. No such invasions occurred in 1989; the absence of Soviet force, not its failure, is what mattered.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Gorbachev did not build walls; the existing one was torn down by the crowds his non-intervention enabled.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, two years after the Eastern European revolutions.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It identifies the decisive change: the repudiation of the Brezhnev Doctrine removed the threat that had kept the satellite regimes in power.

items.fact_source: u9.md §Key terms — End of the Cold War: 'the 1989–1991 collapse of Soviet power in Eastern Europe and the USSR's dissolution'

items.stem: After 1991, some commentators declared the 'end of history' — the permanent triumph of liberal democracy over all rivals. Which later development best challenges that claim?
options: (A) Great-power rivalry returned, authoritarian states endured, and Western democracies polarized deeply after 2010.
(B) The complete disappearance of all authoritarian governments by the year 2000.
(C) The unanimous global adoption of American-style democracy, with every nation converting during the 1990s without a single exception anywhere.
(D) The end of all international conflict after the Cold War ended.
items.explanation: The 'end of history' thesis mistook a moment for a destination. The decades after 1991 brought a more assertive Russia and China, authoritarian regimes that survived and adapted, and — as the review stresses — institutional distrust and polarization inside the United States itself, including the January 6 attack on the Capitol. Liberal democracy's victory was neither complete nor permanent.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It cites the actual record the review describes — the failure to build a new consensus, polarization, institutional distrust — as evidence against permanent triumph.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Authoritarian governments persisted and in some cases strengthened after 1991; they did not disappear.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. No such unanimous adoption occurred; many states adopted democratic forms briefly or not at all.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The post–Cold War era saw the Gulf War, the Balkans, Afghanistan, Iraq, and many other conflicts.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — 'The through-line of the whole period is the end of the Cold War consensus about America's role in the world — and the failure, so far, to build a new one'

items.stem: The chart shows U.S. military spending at $299 billion in 1990, higher than its 1988 level of $290 billion. What does this suggest about the 'peace dividend' many Americans expected after the Cold War?

chart_spec.title: U.S. Military Spending, 1980–1990 (nominal)
chart_spec.source_note: Approximate figures; the Reagan-era military buildup described in u9.md §The story ('spending massively on the military abroad').

options: (A) The peace dividend arrived immediately and completely, with American military spending falling all the way to zero in 1990, ending the defense budget entirely.
(B) The dividend disappointed: spending held near Cold War peaks as the USSR collapsed, and new interventions added fresh demands.
(C) Military spending had never risen in the first place, so no dividend was possible.
(D) The chart proves the Cold War never actually ended.
items.explanation: The chart shows the buildup's momentum carrying past the Cold War's end: 1990 spending was the highest plotted. Some cuts did come in the 1990s, but the Gulf War, the Balkans, and later Afghanistan and Iraq kept America globally entangled — the 'victory lap' never produced the deep demobilization many had imagined.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The chart shows $299 billion in 1990, the highest value plotted — not zero and not falling.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It reads the chart accurately (spending still at peak as the USSR collapsed) and connects it to the interventions that absorbed the would-be savings.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The chart documents a dramatic rise from $134 to $299 billion; the buildup plainly happened.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The Cold War's end is dated by the review to 1989–1991; high spending afterward reflects institutional momentum and new missions, not a continuing Soviet threat.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — America 'stood alone as the unchallenged superpower, and the 1990s felt like a victory lap'; Gulf War (1991)

items.stem: Which internal development most directly caused the Soviet Union itself — not just its Eastern European satellites — to dissolve in December 1991?
options: (A) Independence movements in the Baltics, Ukraine, and beyond hollowed out the union from within.
(B) The United States invaded the Soviet Union in 1991 and dissolved it by force.
(C) Gorbachev abolished the entire Soviet military, leaving the vast country completely defenseless against invasion.
(D) The Soviet economy was booming, so the republics saw no reason to remain.
items.explanation: The USSR was a multi-ethnic empire, and glasnost uncorked nationalisms the party had suppressed for decades. As Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Ukraine, and others declared sovereignty, Moscow's authority evaporated republic by republic; by December 1991 there was no union left for Gorbachev to preside over, whatever Washington did or didn't do.

option_explanations.A: Correct. It identifies the proximate internal mechanism: secessionist nationalism dissolving the federation from inside, the distinct final step after Eastern Europe's breakaway.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The United States never invaded the Soviet Union; the dissolution was an internal political collapse.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Gorbachev kept the armed forces intact; they simply would not — and could not — hold the union together.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The economy was stagnating badly; economic failure fueled the republics' exit rather than preventing it.

items.stem: With the Soviet Union gone, the review says America 'stood alone as the unchallenged superpower.' What did this unipolar moment mean for American foreign policy in the 1990s?
options: (A) The United States withdrew from the world and adopted strict isolationism.
(B) American foreign policy became identical to Soviet foreign policy in every respect, goal, and method.
(C) The United Nations was abolished as unnecessary in the new era.
(D) The U.S. faced fewer great-power constraints after 1991 and undertook interventions to uphold a liberal order.
items.explanation: Unipolarity removed the Soviet veto — literal, at the UN, and strategic, in every crisis. Washington used that freedom to lead coalitions against Iraq and later in the Balkans, presenting American power as the enforcer of a rules-based order. The 'new world order' was unipolarity's doctrine: one superpower managing the peace.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The 1990s were an active interventionist decade, the opposite of isolationism.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. American policy pursued liberal-order goals alien to Soviet practice; the two were not interchangeable.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The UN remained central — the Gulf War was fought under its authorization — and was not abolished.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It captures what unipolarity enabled: American-led collective action without a rival bloc to block or balance it.

items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — America 'stood alone as the unchallenged superpower, and the 1990s felt like a victory lap: the Gulf War (1991) expelled Iraq from Kuwait in weeks'
